...and broken covenants. Because of this, I thought it necessary to describe this Declaration of mine before my other writings and to prove it with examples. My goal is so that everyone whom God judges worthy may conceive, understand, and fathom the true beginning, the true middle, and the true end of all created things.

Consequently, I intended to begin with a necessary account of the origin, beginning, and existence of **minerals** and **metals**. From these arises this most noble and precious **Medicine** <note>likely referring to the Philosopher’s Stone or a universal healing elixir</note>, through which a healthy long life is secured and abundant riches are obtained. Specifically, I will explain where **minerals** and **metals** originate and how they are brought to light. This is so that those who search into natural things may understand the whole scope of **Nature** before they ever start their work and become well-acquainted with it. Then, one discovery will naturally flow into the next, and one **art** <note>original: "Art"; here referring to a practical skill or alchemical process</note> will produce another. At last, everything being sought will be joyfully achieved, and what has been longed for will be happily enjoyed.

I have divided this book into five parts, each of which is subdivided into specific chapters and sections. As for the style used here, you should not expect anything other than what is appropriate for a **miner**, according to the conditions of **mining operations**, setting aside all rhetoric and poetic forms of eloquent expression.

In the first part of my planned work, I will chiefly describe the manner, nature, and properties of **mining operations** in which **minerals** and **metals** grow. I will discuss their "first sperm" <note>original: "sperm"; in this context, the primordial "seed" or fundamental substance from which metals were thought to grow</note>, birth, quality, and properties, as well as their exhalations and inhalations <note>original: "exhalation and inhalation"; referring to the Early Modern theory that minerals were formed by vapors and fumes trapped within the earth</note>.

## II.

*The second part shall be a kind of summary <note>original: "recapitulation"</note> of the first part, which will also contain an account of the condition and occurrence of* Mines, Ores <note>original: "Oars"</note>, Stones, *passages, and crevices, along with their associated liquids, powers, and operations—such as those of* Gold, Silver, Copper, Iron, Tin, Lead, Mercury, *and the rest of the* Minerals.

## III.

*In the third part, I declare in clear and literal expressions, without any flaw or obscurity, the* Universal <note>The "Universal" refers to the *Materia Prima* or the fundamental substance of the alchemical world.</note> *of this whole world: how all* Philosophers <note>In this context, "Philosophers" refers to alchemists, practitioners of the "Hermetic Philosophy."</note> *before me, alongside me, and after me have made that most ancient Great Stone <note>The Philosopher's Stone, the legendary substance capable of transmuting base metals into gold and providing a universal cure for illness.</note>, through which health and riches were obtained. Keys <note>The "Twelve Keys of Basil Valentine" is a famous alchemical text describing the process of creating the Philosopher's Stone through symbolic allegories.</note>, *including the names of our matter.*

## IV.

This fourth part I have titled the* Manuals *of* Basilius Valentinus, *in which is shown how all* Metals and Minerals *suitable for this purpose may be brought to their highest state of preparation.*

### CHAPTER I.
### *Of the Ethereal liquor of Metals, or of the metal Ferch.*
<note>original: "Ferch". In alchemical literature, "Ferch" or "Fercho" refers to the internal spirit, soul, or "archeus" of a metal—the vital force that allows it to grow within the earth.</note>

**G**od has created things underground as well as things above ground. By things underground, I mean metals and minerals, in which a fertility is also implanted within their seed; without this, the seed could neither grow nor increase. Seed which is barren does not have that fertility. From this, it is gathered that there is a distinction between seed and fertility. If we wish to inquire closely into what fertility is, the best and surest way is to consider the life and death of creatures and how they relate to one another; for death is barren, but a living life is fertile because it stirs and moves.

It is evident from all the works performed upon metals that nothing is as volatile <note>In alchemy, "volatile" refers to a substance that easily vaporizes or is "spirited," representing the active, non-fixed principle of a material.</note> as metal is, and so nothing stirs and moves more subtly than it. But this stirring and moving I

<summary>In this opening chapter, Basilius Valentinus introduces the concept of the "Ferch" or ethereal spirit of metals, arguing that minerals possess a vital, fertile seed similar to living creatures.</summary>
<keywords>Basilius Valentinus, alchemy, metallurgy, Ferch, ethereal liquor, mineral seed, fertility of metals, volatility</keywords>

# Basilius Valentinus's Last [Will and Testament]

...I will call here the *Ferch* <note>original: "Ferch"; a term used by Valentine to describe an internal, vital life-force or spirit within matter</note> of metals, by reason of its continual proceeding and incessant moving; and because the same is not visible in metals and does it in a twofold way, therefore I will let the old word stand and call its stirring a *Lubricum* <note>original: "Lubricum"; Latin for slippery or smooth, here referring to the fluid, moving quality of the metal’s spirit</note>, and its *Ferch* a *Volatile* <note>original: "Volatile"; a substance that easily evaporates or changes state when heated</note>; for with the virtue and power of both these, it performs all that which it needs for the perfection, purity, and fixation <term>The alchemical process of making a volatile substance solid or stable so that it can withstand heat without evaporating.</term> of its work.

Since *Ferch* is a perpetual, living, and active thing, one might wonder and say: what is the condition of metal then, which we behold with our eyes and feel with our hands? Which, being thus hard and solidified, is it alive or dead? And whether the life or *Ferch* in metals may be destroyed (which is impossible), what is its condition, or how does it happen? 

I answer that a metal may be alive when it rests, just as well as when it grows or moves; and here a distinction must be made again between the death of metals and their rest and quietness. For death touches only the bodies when they perish, but the life itself, or *Ferch*, cannot perish or cease. Therefore, if a metallic body exists, then it is present visibly in two ways. The one is in a *liquid* state <note>original: "liquidum"</note>, and is perceived in its moving to and fro; and if it is forced by an external, intense heat, then it turns into a volatility and flies away. The other way is when it is present in *coagulato* <note>original: "coagulato"; Latin for a coagulated or solid state</note>, in which it rests so long until it is reduced into its *liquidum* <note>original: "liquidum"; Latin for a liquid or fluid state</note>; and that is done in a twofold way and lasts as long as the body lasts. But as soon as the body is destroyed or gone, and has come or entered into either a more noble <note>Higher quality, such as gold</note> or ignoble <note>Lower quality, such as lead</note> body, then its *Ferch* or life is

<meta>catchword: gone</meta>

<summary>Basilius Valentinus defines the vital life-force of metals, which he calls "Ferch," explaining that this spirit persists in both solid and liquid states and cannot be destroyed, only moved between bodies.</summary>
<keywords>Basilius Valentinus, Ferch, alchemy, Lubricum, Volatile, fixation, coagulation, metalline body, vitalism</keywords>

<meta>This page continues a discussion on the preservation of a "body" (likely in an alchemical or philosophical sense) by managing its vital spirit or internal life force.</meta>

<page-num>3</page-num>
->*Will and Testament.*<-
<sig>B 2</sig>

...is gone also. Therefore, if you wish to reserve and keep a body, then take careful notice of its *Ferch* <note>original: "Ferch"; likely a term for the vital spirit, internal fire, or life-force, possibly derived from Welsh or a specific alchemical jargon</note> or life. For if you once disturb it and hunt it indiscreetly, you do so at the loss or weakening of the body in which it resides. That life never departs empty-handed; it continually carries away one life or *Ferch* after another, carrying it away for so long that, at last, it leaves nothing behind. 

But the conditions of the movement and quietness of that life, and how Nature brings it to a rest, must be precisely considered. Accurate knowledge demonstrates that there is a difference between the life of the "seed" and the life of the "body." Deal with the seed in whatever way you will, you cannot bring it to a state of *volatility* <note>original: "volatility"; in alchemy, the quality of a substance that allows it to be easily evaporated or changed into vapor</note> because that is against its nature. The body is in the same condition; however, the *Ferch* alone may be brought to volatility. 

If you provide food for the *Ferch*, then you strengthen its entire work, just as a mother feeds and cherishes her child well to bring it more easily to its rest; so it is also with the *Ferch*. Therefore, all those who only gaze at and view the seed and the body, but do not know the fundamentals concerning the *Ferch*, lose the body because they do not observe Nature's progress and proceedings. They put the cart before the horse, or put the first things last. 

This rest and "sleep" of the *Ferch* serves a specific use: it preserves the body from destruction or consumption once it has reached its perfection. As long as it is "awake," it consumes; but when it is at rest, it remains stable in a state of durability. When it has nothing else to feed upon, it corrodes and seizes its own body, consuming it entirely. At last, it stirs and moves—

<summary>This page explains the importance of the "Ferch" (vital life-force) in preserving a physical body or alchemical substance, warning that mismanagement of this spirit leads to the body's destruction. It emphasizes that the spirit must be "nourished" and brought to rest to prevent it from consuming its own host body.</summary>

...to another place. This is why treasures or valuables <note>original: "pagement," likely referring to buried wealth or pavements</note> which are buried eventually awaken, consume their own bodies, and reduce them to dust, so that nothing remains of them except either a mere stone or flux <note>original: "flux"; a substance used to promote melting or the state of being fluid</note>, as can be seen in many places.

## CHAP. II.

### Of the Seed of Metals.

**A**ll those authors who have written about the <term>metallic seed</term> agree in this: they say <term>Sulphur</term> is the masculine seed of metals, and <term>Mercury</term> is the feminine seed. However, this saying must be understood in its true sense, for ordinary sulphur and ordinary mercury are not meant by it. The visible mercury of metals is a body itself, derived from other bodies, and so it cannot be a seed. Furthermore, being cold, its coldness in itself <note>original: "per se"</note> cannot be a seed; and since the sulphur of metals is a food, how can it be a seed? Indeed, a seed consumes sulphur; how can one seed destroy the other? If so, what body could it produce?

It is therefore an error if that is understood in the common sense. If the mercury of bodies is used in a work and has taken food, then all the six <note>original: "sex," likely meaning the six metals other than the one being produced</note> mercuries produce one body; as one of the types <note>original: "sex"</note> is predominant, so the body arises.

# Of Basil Valentine.

Therefore **I** will instruct you here to make only some preparations, which also are required to other things.

Take pure Mineral <term>Antimony</term> <note>A semi-metallic element that was central to alchemical medicine, believed to have powerful purifying properties when correctly prepared.</note>, which is brought from *Hungary*, grind it small, and wash it very clean, so that the earth may be separated from it. Add to this metallic heart its weight of <term>Nitre</term>, and melt it down. Pour it out together, and beat off the <term>dross</term> <note>original: "Scoriæ" — the stony or glassy waste matter separated from metals during smelting.</note>, and put again to the metallic heart its weight of <term>Nitre</term>, and melt it. Repeat this until all the metallic heart has turned into dross, which you must carefully keep: they will burn upon the tongue like fire. 

This being done, take the matter so gathered, grind it small, and <term>wash away the salt</term> <note>original: "edulcorate" — to wash a solid with water to remove any remaining acids or salts.</note> from it, and there remains a brown-yellow powder; dry this and keep it, for it looks like ground glass. Take now a common metallic heart of <term>Antimony</term>, made with <term>Salt-peter</term> and <term>Tartar</term>, grind it small, and put it into a round glass vessel, which must not be too high, and fasten a "Head" <note>An alembic or still-head used to collect vapors.</note> to it. <term>Vaporize and collect</term> <note>original: "Sublime" — to heat a solid so it turns into vapor and then solidifies again in a purer form.</note> your metallic heart in a sand bath by itself without any addition. # CHAPTER 3

## *On the Nutriment of Metals*

**A**lthough it does not belong in this section to explain how fossilized minerals <note>original: *mineralia fossilia*, referring generally to anything dug out of the earth</note> are made underground, I will nonetheless give a hint as to how nature makes them out of moist subterranean fluids and mineral growths <note>original: "Myne crescencies"</note>. These later serve as food for metals. These are not the same as the liquors distilled or boiled above ground; therefore, if you were to add such liquids prepared above ground to metals that remain in their solid, physical form, your work would be in vain. Miners very seldom know—especially in *Hungary* and *Wallachia* <note>Wallachia: a historical region of present-day Romania</note>—that these ores are as beautiful as any red glowing ore can be. The preparation of these "flowers" <term>flowers: in early chemistry, these were powders or sublimates produced by heating a substance</term> is of great utility in medicinal <note>original: "physical"</note> ways, provided their "excrements" and odors are removed. Mistaking these minerals leads to a twofold evil. First, those that have been decocted <term>decocted: boiled or heated to extract essence</term> become a dangerous poison and are corrosive to metals. Second, others that appear beautiful but cling to the metals are their worst poison. As soon as these approach the metal, they ignite and cause dangerous sediments; it profits the metal nothing, even if they retain their outward form. Just as an infected person still has the form and face of a human despite being diseased and infecting others, so too if a substance turns entirely into one metal, it may remain "empty" and worthless inside.

If they do not pay attention to this, they not only hinder their work but also endanger themselves. ## Chapter IV.

### Of the Metallic Workshop, *Officina metallorum* <note>Latin: workshop of metals</note>.

**A**ll natural processes have their specific, suitable places in which they operate. Wherever there is such a place or shop in which some glorious and precious thing is made—and sometimes even though the instrument used is very horrid and monstrous and its material unknown—they still exist in that workshop <note>original: "officine"</note>.

If it must be parted asunder, then see and test it on the mercury of metals.

It is like water that flows around a stone and not through it; yet it stays within its own stone, receives strength from it, and there turns into a solid body. Something may be obtained more easily and quickly from slippery things than from hard things; slippery things always leave something behind. They do the same with their tinting bodies <note>original: "tinging bodies," referring to the alchemical "tincture" or essence that changes the nature/color of a substance</note>, shedding them in such a way that, as they rise in their *volatile* state, they take up the body and elevate it.

Note: if you have any material in hand and wish to know in your subsequent work <note>original: "After-work"</note> whether you must rely on the *lubricity* or the *volatility* (for these two must be your aids), then your material must be prepared either in the slippery or the volatile way. If you want a body to either ascend <note>evaporate or sublime</note> or descend <note>condense or precipitate</note>, observe the flux <term>the state of being fluid or a substance added to promote melting</term> in the metal. Slippery metals are more "open" <note>porous or chemically reactive</note> than hard ones. When tinctures begin to depart—which act as a strengthener—the material becomes more fluid and compact than it was in its "quick" <note>living or raw metallic</note> state.

## CHAP. X.

### Of pure or fine Metal.

When a metal—whether it is in a state of ascension or descension <note>Early modern miners believed metals "grew" or moved within the earth; "ascension" and "descension" refer to the movement of metallic vapors or fluids through the Earth's crust.</note>—is in its seven systems <note>original: "System’s"; likely referring to the seven classical metals associated with the seven planets.</note> or its proper constitution, it remains stable until it is incorporated into another body. If you find such ore, it yields the purest metal that can be found in the world. Our smelters call this "Super-fine." However, the "super-fining" process used until now is an imperfect work compared to this; for in the refining process, if it misses by even the smallest grain, it is not yet correct. Such metals, as can easily be understood, are pure, good, and malleable, losing nothing during any kind of craftsmanship. Although all metals may be refined to a "super-fine" state, none can be made finer than gold. No element is able to damage gold, take anything from it, or turn it into *glimmer* (Latin: *spolium* <note>In this context, *spolium* refers to waste, dross, or the "spoils" of the refining process.</note>) or "cat-silver" <note>original: "cats-silver"; a period term for mica or other glittering but worthless minerals.</note>, which has a glittering quality but no value.

Silver from Marychurch in Lorraine <note>original: "Marychurch at Lorrayne"; referring to Sainte-Marie-aux-Mines, a famous silver mining district in France.</note> is finer than others. A metal is called "super-fine" when it is pure and cleared of its impurities or dross, which can be easily removed and does not hinder the refining process. In silver mines, natural examples of such pure and fine ore are often found. This ore can be quickly dug and broken, though it must be melted again because of its *spolium* (waste) or because of the strange colors and "flowers" it has absorbed. Yet, this melting is easily performed and serves as a guide for how mineral colors must be obtained—such as Azure and Chrysocolla <note>original: "Chryfocolle"; a hydrated copper silicate mineral used as a blue-green pigment.</note>—even though they are found within the mineral glass <note>A term for the crystalline or vitreous matrix in which minerals are embedded.</note>. ## CHAPTER XI.

### Of Impure Metal.

**A** great abundance of metallic ores <note>original: "metalline oars"</note> is found, but few of them are pure, and few grow together in a single vein; therefore, these must be separated and discussed individually. Let the smelters <note>original: "Melters"</note> speak of the great effort and expense required to cleanse them of their impurities <note>original: "grossenesse"</note>. Techniques for separation have been invented through which the valuable parts of the ore remain while the rest is lost. Refining <note>original: "fining"</note> them is useful, especially when ores or metals are in their state of transformation <note>original: "ascension," referring to the alchemical process of vaporizing or rising</note>, though it is expensive <note>original: "chargeable"</note>. 

However, finding *Electrums* <note>a natural alloy of gold and silver</note> and refining them differs from standard refining and requires a unique method of smelting. Clever and deceptive alchemists <note>original: "subtile Artists"</note> may claim to extract silver from iron—and I believe they can, if there is any actually in it—as they do in Sweden <note>original: "Sweedland"</note>. Osmund iron <note>original: "Osemund," a high-quality Swedish iron produced in small lumps</note> always contains silver; however, they simply extract it by burning away <note>original: "calcine"</note> the iron, and thus they cheat people. Can they do the same with the iron found in Styria <note>a region in modern-day Austria famous for its iron mountain</note>? Certainly not. 

Therefore, beware of such frauds. Observe that nature prefers to follow her own orderly paths, keeping two and sometimes three types of ore together during their formation <note>original: "ascension and descension"</note>. By doing this, nature suggests the proper method for further processing <note>original: "After-work"</note>; yet men, in their vanity, imagine other methods that are ultimately useless.

And this is the second argument: that metals are in a state of ascension and descension toward perfection. <note>In alchemical theory, metals were believed to "grow" in the earth, moving from "imperfect" states like lead toward "perfection" as gold.</note> If each metal were produced by its own unique process and instrument, then men would not need to take such great pains in smelting to separate them. # CHAPTER 12
## *Of perfect metal.*

Who could tell what gold and silver were if they were not known in their perfection? For when they are perfect, it is apparent; they show their color, their weight, their malleability <note>original: "malleableness"</note>, their flux <term>flux</term> <note>In metallurgy, the state of being liquid or the ability of a metal to flow when heated.</note>, and their hardness. Nature has produced this perfect metal compactly and purely; for such perfect, pure, and compact gold is found in Hungary in white marble, which may be readily broken, as may silver and copper. The difference between the "perfect" and the "pure" is that metals are not pure before they are perfect; therefore, there may be a perfect ore <note>original: "oar"</note> which is not pure. This defect is found in many of our metals, which reach their perfection as soon as those in any other foreign parts, but they are sometimes defective in their perfect purity. ## CHAP. XIII.

### On Imperfect Metals.

**I**mperfect metal is the wildest among all the rest, because it contains all impurities in a confused mixture. Usually, it is found in a work of many parts, the nature of which no one yet knows, in which you find substances joined together that are both refined and unrefined from many different "bodies" <note>In alchemy, "bodies" refers to the solid metallic forms of elements.</note>. Now, if you wish to refine that matter and cleanse its metal, then the unrefined matter must first be washed away. Do not focus as much on the raw matter as on the metal itself, which is still tender and young within it. You must not calcine it <note>original: calcine; to reduce a substance to a powdery ash through dry heat</note>, for a different kind of fire is required for it. This process of perfection consists of nine distinct steps which must be carefully considered; each must be handled exactly as it should be if the metal is to escape harm or damage.

First, consider well whether the <term>ore</term> <note>original: oar</note> is in "ascension" or "descension" <note>These terms likely refer to the spiritual or physical state of the metal during its growth in the earth or its reaction in the flask.</note>; then you may improve its color and its entire body. For that metal which is in its ascension must be aided in its *folium* <note>Latin: leaf; likely referring to the thin layers or surface of the metal</note>, but the metal which is in its descension must be helped with *spolium* <note>Latin: spoil or residue</note>. Otherwise, it dies away because it is not perfected in its proper place and *officina* <note>Latin: workshop or laboratory</note>; that metal takes its form accordingly. Conduct your trial in this way, and you will be more encouraged in your later work.

Secondly, you must take notice of the nourishment or "food" which, so to speak, is not yet fully digested. Promote this in its <term>concoction</term> <note>original: concoction; the process of "ripening" or purifying a substance through steady heat</note>; otherwise, the impurities <note>original: excrements</note> cannot be easily removed.

### CHAP. XIV.

#### *Of the Soap-metal, or Metallum Uredinum.*

**I**f our upper elements could not make a metal manifest and apparent to us, who would have undertaken to work with any metal? ## CHAPTER XV.

### *Of inhalation or inbreathing.*

**I**t is an intricate work to build secondary fissures and passages, for it seems believable that the "breathings" move in and out through them more than through the rest of the earth. However, it is not advisable to take such roundabout routes, because there is a nearer way to reach the metals. It is as if one wanted to go to a well and followed all the streams down through every spring, when there is a nearer way by taking the footpath. The same condition applies to the <term>exhalations</term><note>original: "halations"; the vapors or "breaths" emitted by minerals</note> and breathings, because the fumes and vapors lie within those passages and are an obstruction to the breathing rather than a help. Therefore, do not look so much at the clefts and passages, but rather at the exhalations or breathings which maintain their path throughout the earth, because the earth itself does not hinder their course, as men may assume. For we must know that the <term>ores</term><note>original: "oars"</note> "breathe" only underground, and these breathings are orderly

# CHAP. XVIII.

## *Of Folium and Spolium; or of the Shimmer and Glimmer.*
<note>original: *Folium & Spolium*; literally "Leaf and Spoil," likely referring to the surface "leaf" or sheen of a metal and the residue or "spoil" left after processing</note>

**T**he second or other thing which clearly shows and distinguishes metals is the color. The nature of color is such that metals are not easily discernible because of their natural darkness. They are elevated and brought to a <term>*Folium*</term> <note>original: *Folium*; Latin for "leaf," referring to the thin, shining surface or "foil" of a metal</note>, or are exalted through a <term>folium</term>, just as an obscure and non-transparent <term>folium</term> acts within a <term>bright and translucent body</term> <note>original: *lucidum & translucidum corpus*</note>. The same must a transparent <term>folium</term> do in a thick body, as metals are an <term>opaque body</term> <note>original: *opacum corpus*</note>, shining like the moon with a borrowed light into the body, and the <term>folium</term> reflects it out of that body.

Such a <term>folium</term> or glitter may be made artificially, but nature shows that it may be obtained from a <term>volatile substance</term> <note>original: *Volatile*; a substance that easily evaporates or changes state, often central to alchemical transformation</note>. Though it is true that this <term>volatile substance</term> may not be obtained except within its seed and body, yet it is soon present with the body. ## CHAPTER XX.

### *Of scrapings <note>original: Scobes</note> and metallic water, of the crushed ore <note>original: Schlich</note> and lye (Lixivium).*

**N**ature in her work must always have an increase and decrease; some things are coming, and others are going. And just as metals lose something above ground during melting and under the hammer, so it is underground. But how are these underground losses discerned? Like crumbs of bread, they should be preserved. Nature, being provident, keeps them together as well, bringing them to the light of day so that they might be put to good use. The presence of metal is also known to be under that ground by the scrapings <note>original: *Scobs*; filings or dross</note> or salt <note>original: *Alkali*</note> which it excretes: namely, the rocks, stones, and flints which sucked Nature dry in her work. ## CHAPTER XXII.
### *Of the shining rod, or of the fire rod.*

He who intends to work with rods must not follow his own fancy, nor bring novelties into the mines based on his own guesses. For nature does not allow herself to be restrained in her order; rather, men must be regulated according to nature. Concerning the rod, careful notice must be taken of the "Breathing" <note>In mining lore, "breathing" refers to the vapors or exhalations rising from mineral veins in the earth.</note>, and this *shining rod* <note>original: "Lucens virgula"</note> or fire-rod is governed by this active and attractive breathing. For if the breathing is strong, even if the rod does not ignite, it still performs its function through a heat suited to its quality. Just as a great heat in a furnace puts out a small heat, light, or fire, this breathing has the same effect upon this rod. When the rod is lit and thrust in, it is extinguished; no surface air or wind can harm it, for our surface fire cannot live or burn...

### CHAPTER XXIII.

### *Regarding the Glowing Rod.*

**B**ecause the use of the dowsing rod <note>original: "stirring of the Rod"</note> has fallen into abuse among many people, it is nevertheless a fundamental way to identify and bring forth metals if it is used correctly and naturally. It is an undeniable truth, as I mentioned previously, that metals "breathe," and this same breathing is invisible. The best way to detect it is with the rod; this is the reason why I call this tool the "glowing rod." It reveals and shows the exhalation of metals, and this exhalation consists of a fiery heat. Although it casts neither flame nor sparks, it is of such a heat that it glows in its own manner and causes the rod to glow, which is an infallible sign that a living metal is nearby. 

If this rod is to glow more intensely without a flame, a special substance must be used which receives that fire; otherwise, it cannot be done with any usefulness. # CHAP. XXIV.

### *Of the leaping Rod.*

**W**hile metal is undergoing its purification, so that it neither rises nor moves, it then possesses its "breathing." Because this breathing is of a unique condition, it must be discovered and released by a special rod. This rod consists of two sticks held together with both hands. Wherever such a breathing exists, it presses closely against that rod; no man is able to hold these sticks together if that breathing acts upon them. Indeed, if it were a single stick, it would break in two. 

The inner side, where this rod is joined together, must be anointed with marcasite <note>original: "Marcasite"; in this period, the term referred to various metallic sulfides like pyrite or bismuth, believed to have a magnetic-like attraction to certain metals</note>. That breathing draws the rod downward, just as a magnet has an attractive quality that draws iron; so the breathing of this ore <note>original: "oar"</note> draws the marcasite, because the nature and property of the marcasite is to strengthen the breathing of the purification. 

There is no better way of refining than to use the specific marcasite peculiar to each metal. There is a twofold marcasite: one from above, originating from the *Uredines* <note>original: "Uredines"; likely referring to atmospheric or celestial "blasting" heats or elemental forces</note> (or upper elemental heat), and the other from the depths below. From this marcasite, a <term>Schlich</term> <note>original: "Schlich"; a technical term for finely crushed ore or metallic dust that has been washed and prepared for smelting</note> or small dust is applied to the point of the rod. The metal's breathing then causes the rod to leap asunder. 

During the melting of ores and metals, a double "slack" <note>likely referring to slag or a fluxing agent used to separate impurities</note> must be added—both an upper and a lower—so that the metal may "bleak" <note>likely meaning to shine, clarify, or become pale/pure</note> better. The same must be observed here during this purifying and refining. Because marcasites (especially those from above, rather than those from underground) carry "soap-metal" <note>possibly a reference to minerals found in alluvial deposits or a substance that "washes" the metal</note> and are pure, they assist the purification very much. ## CHAPTER XXVI.

### Concerning the *Virgula Trepidans*; or the Heaving or Trembling Rod.

**S**ince the "breathings" <note>term: Alchemical exhalations or vapors believed to flow through the earth and influence the growth of metals</note> drive the fumes together from both above and below, you must understand that it requires great skill to distinguish these from other types of vapors. The vapors of the upper element are Jovial <note>original: "jovial," referring to the influence of the planet Jupiter, which in alchemy is associated with the element of air and the metal tin</note>, and the lower vapors are Jovial as well; this is clearly seen in their effects. The wind is also governed by *Jupiter*; he mixes these fumes together, and that specific vapor can hardly be detected by the rod. This skill is of a very high level.

This heaving rod shows the way. It must be made of a metallic plate, such as steel, which must be thrust beneath the damp earth <note>original: "dam earth," referring to moist soil or a specific layer of earth that contains moisture</note>. At the edge of that earth, these vapors and exhalations meet, and the rod stirs and quakes—which it will not do unless it is at such a location and time. 

The rays of the lower and upper bodies cannot be stopped, except where they are actively working; for as they "breathe," they rise and fall, and they are not interrupted in their natural flow unless they encounter the material of this rod. There is a knot on that stick, and it is hollow like a cane. The material of this rod is made of *Electrum* <note>term: In this context, an alchemical alloy of gold and silver</note>, drawn from the finest thin plates of *Luna* (silver) and *Sol* (gold). This is placed into a glass head, which does not block the vapors—because they cannot be obstructed as easily as they might be by a vessel made above ground. Therefore, be careful how you proceed: you may fail if you drive it in too deep, or if you do not extract material from the lower earth as was mentioned previously.

## CHAPTER XXXI.

### Concerning *Metallic Whetstone* <note>original: "Cos metallicus"</note> or *stone-salt*.

**T**he air, being formed from a portion of pure earth, eventually turns into stone. There are several sorts of stones, just as there are several bodies in the earth, though all of them are merely earth. The longer the matter remains there, the harder and richer <note>original: "fatter"; in alchemy, this implies a higher concentration of "sulfur" or mineral essence</note> it will be. Such stones cannot be moved or lifted except by fire, which seizes the earth, consumes it, and turns it into a terrestrial firmament—similar to how scales are found on fish and bones in beasts. The Lord will also consume these with fire in His own good time. 

This motivated the ancients to consume their corpses with fire; although flesh soon rots underground, the bones do not decay so quickly. Fire consumes them, turning them into earth-ashes.

## CHAPTER VI.

### *Of the Spirit of Gold.*

**T**he brightness of Heaven has now commanded me to change my pen, to discover a thing of fortitude and of constancy, because the Sun is a burning, consuming fire—hot and dry—wherein there is a true power of all natural things. This power of the Sun works wisdom, riches, and health. My heart is seized by sorrow, and my spirit within itself becomes astonished to manifest and bring to light such things as have not been discovered and commonly laid open before me, and to reveal that which has been buried in the depth with very great secrecy.

# CHAP. VII.

## Of the Tincture of Silver.

**T**he tincture and spirit of silver is sky-blue; otherwise, it is a watery spirit, cold and moist, and not as hot in its nature <note>original: "degree"</note> as the spirit found in gold, iron, or copper. Therefore, silver is more phlegmatic <note>A term from humoral theory meaning cool and moist.</note> than fiery, even though it has been solidified <note>original: "reduced... unto a coagulation"</note> from its watery substance by fire. In the same way that metals obtain their coloring <note>original: "tinging"</note> spirits and solidity, gemstones have likewise received their hardness, stability, and color through the very same influences. 

In a diamond, one finds a stable <note>original: "fixed"</note> and solidified mercury; therefore, this stone is harder and more stable than other stones and cannot be broken as they can. In a ruby, one finds the tincture of iron, or the sulfur of iron. In an emerald <note>original: "Esmerauld"</note>, the tincture of copper; in a garnet <note>original: "Granate"</note>, the soul <note>The OCR reads "foul," likely a misreading of the Early Modern long "s." In alchemy, the "soul" (anima) refers to the internal essence or color.</note> of lead. In tin <note>original: "Pewter," which in this period often referred to the metal tin.</note>, the tincture found in the stone called topaz <note>original: "Topasius"</note>. Crystal is attributed to common mercury. And in a sapphire <note>original: "Saphir"</note>, one finds the tincture and sulfur of silver—yet each thing remains distinct according to its own nature and type, just as it is with the various forms of metals. 

When the blue color is separated and removed from the sapphire, then its "garment" <note>its outward appearance or color</note> is gone, and its body is white like a diamond. Similarly, when gold has lost its soul <note>OCR: "foul."</note>, it then yields a white body—a stable white gold which is called *Luna fixa* <note>Latin: "fixed moon," referring to a version of gold that has been made to appear like silver or silver that has been stabilized.</note> by the

[Nature] has planted this quality into the second creature and into the second planet of the Earth—namely, into **Silver**. All things are hard and difficult in the beginning; but once they are brought to completion, they are easy to understand and comprehend.
